To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dementia patients incur significantly higher costs than age-matched control subjects, that women and men incur similar total costs but that women account for lower health care and higher long-term care costs than men, and that total costs of dementia care increase in older age, whereas health care costs decrease.

(i) dementia is associated with higher costs for health and long-term services, (ii) these costs are higher in older ages, (iii) women incur higher long-term care costs than men, and (iv) women incur lower health care costs than men.

the excess costs of dementia are high and increase with age, that the additional costs of dementia care are higher for women than for men, and that the long-term care system is more severely challenged by dementia than the health care system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a potential for savings within the social security budget.
the question of whether the German social security budget is capable of meeting the growing need for long-term care services for people with dementia.
the identification of cost drivers and potential areas for cost containment in the care for dementia patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the additional costs of dementia in the long-term-care system are not only higher than in the health care system, but also increase with age, and that women are more affected than men.
dementia care is an important and growing burden on the German social security systems, and that this burden is not equally distributed between men and women.
the German social security systems are challenged by dementia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the German health care system has a lot of room to optimize care for dementia patients.
dementia patients need to get more attention in the health care system and that the health care sector needs to get more attention from policy makers.
dementia is a serious challenge for the social security system in Germany and that women are more vulnerable than men.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the long-term care system should be prepared for a growing demand for care services in an ageing society, especially in view of the fact that the long-term costs of dementia are likely to increase further.
the long-term care system is the most affected sector by dementia.
the German social security systems should be better prepared for the upcoming challenges of demographic ageing.
